agent_notes: מָלָךְ is a perfect, and the verse has no verbs of being: 'YHWH reigns' can be a state ('is king') or an act ('has become king'). YLT takes it as past, KJV/ASV as present. I kept the present state in the literal layer. יִרְגְּזוּ and תָּנוּט are imperfects that can be jussive ('let them') or plain future/present ('they tremble'); KJV/ASV/BBE read a wish, YLT a fact. I glossed them as jussive in the word table and kept 'let' in the literal layer because the parallel opening of Ps 97:1 and 93:1 has no such mood, so the choice is mine.

agent_notes: The verse is syntactically hard. 'And the strength of a king loves justice' (עֹז as subject, אָהֵב as perfect) is the plain reading; KJV/ASV follow it. Rashi takes 'strength' as God's own, tied to 'the Most High' of the previous psalm. I translated literally and kept the doubled 'you' (אַתָּה … אַתָּה), which YLT also keeps. Rashi's reading of מֵישָׁרִים as 'compromise, peace between people' is quoted as his, not adopted.

Revised after the review: literal layer and gloss 11 now render the imperfect יַעֲנֵם as habitual ('he would answer them'), matching the participle 'calling' before it. The commentary no longer ranks YLT above the others; it says the past is also defensible (the imperfect after a participle can be past-habitual), as in KJV/ASV, and that the habitual sense is the one the Hebrew grammar suggests.

בכהניו: STEPBible glosses 'among priests his'; I keep the preposition ב as 'among' (in the company of). Moses as 'priest' rests on Exod 24 and the seven days of ordination (Lev 8), which Ibn Ezra and Radak cite; the Psalm itself does not say it.

Nothing in the Hebrew narrates a cloud for Samuel, so the dramatic layer keeps the pronoun vague.

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: the commentary no longer says 'for the first time in the psalm'. It says that after the third-person narrative of vv. 6-7 the psalm returns to addressing God as 'you', as in vv. 3-4.

STEPBible glosses אֵל as 'a God' and נֹשֵׂא as 'forgiving'. I kept 'forgiving' in the gloss and the dramatic layer, and used 'lifting [up sin]' in the literal layer to show the root. The five English versions split on 'inventions' (KJV, Webster), 'doings' (ASV), 'actions' (YLT) and 'wrongdoing' (BBE) for עֲלִילוֹתָם. I chose 'deeds', the neutral sense of the word, which can be bad or good depending on context.

Who 'them' and the avenged 'deeds' are is disputed. Rashi and Metzudat David read the vengeance as falling on Moses, Aaron and Samuel; Ibn Ezra and Radak link it to Korah's party. The Hebrew does not say, and I left the referents open in the translations and gave both readings in the commentary.
